article_text:
Elon Musk has given $276 million to Republican groups and his super PAC since this July ahead of the midterm elections, the New York Times recently reported . But “ Musk ,” Alex Gibney ‘s documentary about the world’s first trillionaire, is not a political film . Or at least not for the majority of its nearly 4-hour runtime. It’s a film about this singular man’s influence on the world and covers far more ground than his involvement with Trump administration or the midterms.

But the documentary has been treated as political by every social media platform the film has tried to advertise on. Meta and YouTube each pulled distributor Bleecker Street ‘s paid trailer for the film before later restoring it , saying its removal was in error. TikTok on the weekend “Musk” expanded to 500 theaters “permanently” suspended the film’s account because it said it repeatedly violated its policies of paying to boost what it viewed as political content, and it only reinstated the account after two days, an eternity if you’re chasing weekend box office. X, which is owned by Musk, predictably didn’t play ball at all.

Gibney has not been shy highlighting the “accidental” bans that ads for his film have had to endure. His distributor Bleecker Street behind the scenes has been fighting these battles and has been quietly fuming. The film’s box office, just $672K in three weeks, has been extremely disappointing. In response, Bleecker is moving up the PVOD release date of “Musk” to November 6 after slating it for late in November.

And the response has been enormous. Pre-orders for the film, priced at $20, have been outpacing “The Odyssey” on Apple, and it’s among Apple’s top purchased titles even though it doesn’t come out for another week.

“I think it’ll be the most pre-ordered movie in my entire career of doing this,” Kent Sanderson, Bleecker Street CEO , told IndieWire. “People are seeking out the movie. And look, it just may end up being that the experience of a three-hour and-42-minute documentary is something that people wanted to do more at home, but it was our duty to try to maximize the theatrical release in advance of that.”

Sanderson spoke about the constant frustration “Musk” faced in every phase of its advertising cycle, adding that he’s never experienced something to do this degree in his career before (he jokes that he is not expecting Bleecker’s other fall release, Mike Leigh’s “Tender Loving Care,” to experience the same “shadow ban” this film has). Sanderson said not only was it clear that the constant removal of their trailers and teasers was unfair given the film’s broader content, he found that the review and approval process in communication with each of the tech platforms was not as transparent as they would’ve normally expected it to be.

“It just happened over and over again throughout the campaign of assets going up and then being taken down and then going up and then being taken down,” Sanderson said. “The absolute brick wall we hit with TikTok was on the opening Friday of the wide release, and it lasted throughout the weekend.”

Sanderson explained his team would try and amend the situation by editing the trailer to remove footage of Elon at Trump rallies, and the new trailer would still be flagged. The back and forth, he said, was maddening and “constant,” with a whole lot of “this was taken down in error” before the next piece of content would have the same fate. They had better luck with still images or posters rather than anything that was a video, but that’s hardly the way to sell a movie.

“I’m not a conspiracy theorist by nature, but I will say that it was frustrating,” Sanderson said. “It was a frustrating and confusing process for everybody.”

He can’t put a dollar amount on how much the lack of advertising hurt the movie at the box office except to say that it undoubtedly did, but he’s relieved that the movie at least still has some real awareness that has led to the strong pre-sale figures. He’s also not naive to the fact that “Musk” is a tough film for exhibitors to keep on their screens week after week. The movie expanded in a weekend when new movies like “Clayface” and “Wicker” opened and another lengthy documentary, “You Can See Everything,” tripled its screen count , all of which easily could’ve dinged the box office. To keep a four-hour film like “Musk” could mean sacrificing not one but two other titles, and that’s a big ask.

But Sanderson stressed that exhibitors themselves were never hesitant to play the movie, and it wasn’t a fight to get screens for any political reasons. Despite the PVOD release, “Musk” will still play in a few select theaters through this weekend and beyond. He also reassures that he remains in active discussions with HBO and HBO Max about making it available for streaming at a later date, something that people began to doubt after Musk invested $1 billion in the David Ellison-owned Skydance , which now owns HBO.

“I’ve gotten no hesitation from them whatsoever,” he said. “If something’s happening on a higher level, I’m not aware of it.”

Sanderson did want to clarify that though there were some people who wanted to see the film released ahead of the midterm elections next week, this is quite literally the soonest they can turn around the digital release. The PVOD rental will also be available with a slightly extended cut of “Musk” that needed to be delivered, and he also found that the PVOD release window in late November is particularly crowded.

Sanderson confirmed the veracity of a legal letter that Musk’s lawyer sent to Gibney and the film team but said Musk has not contacted Bleecker Street directly. But Sanderson ultimately feels that the suppression of “Musk” is bigger than the impact on this one film or on his individual film company. In the same weekend that “Musk” went wide, the No Kings Rally also had its Instagram account suspended for similar political reasons, and his team has even been talking with that organization about how they’re navigating that same experience.

“It is beyond just the film business. It is about free speech and being able to amplify you’re your message,” Sanderson said. “I understand that there’s a fine line, and you don’t want dangerous content being put out in the world, but this is by definition not dangerous content, and I’m not sure that the social media companies should be the ones to figure out that line.”

“Musk” is in theaters now and is available on PVOD on November 6.

article_text:
Paul Greengrass is known for directing several editions in Universal’s Jason Bourne series. But the filmmaker has said he was once offered the opportunity to decamp and direct a rival James Bond film.

“They asked me after I did Bourne Supremacy ,” Greengrass told The Rest Is Classified podcast.

Greengrass, however, quickly clarified that he would never think of directing a Bond feature.

“I have immense admiration and respect for what Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson did with that. And Daniel, you know, was a fantastic James Bond,” he said. “But it’s a bit like if you play for Manchester United, you can’t sign for Man City, you know? You wouldn’t feel right about that. You feel loyal. I do.”

Greengrass added that he is a certified “Bourne guy”.

Watch on Deadline

“I hope they bring him back. I don’t know whether they will. I think they still try to,” he said.

In June, Matt Damon said he was open to reviving the film series.

“We’re always looking to try to get another one of those because we loved it, everyone who worked on them,” Parade magazine. “So there’s always some attempt going on to write, to come up with a new story. So if you have anything, let us know.”

The Bourne Identity (2002), directed by Doug Liman, was the first in the series. It was followed by The Bourne Supremacy (2004), The Bourne Ultimatum (2007), The Bourne Legacy (2012), and Jason Bourne (2016). Damon did not reprise his role in the fourth entry, which introduced a new character portrayed by Jeremy Renner.

The films have collectively grossed more than $1.64 billion at the global box office.

title_original: Martin Scorsese Recalls His Last Conversation With Federico Fellini in New Doc Premiering at Rome Film Festival: ‘Thank You, I’ll See You Soon’ (EXCLUSIVE)
editorial_title_zh: 马丁·斯科塞斯全新罗马电影节首映纪录片回忆与费德里科·费里尼的最后一次对话：“谢谢你，我们很快会再见”（独家）
editorial_excerpt_zh: 马丁·斯科塞斯在将于周六在罗马电影节首映的全新纪录片《最后的费里尼》（The Last Fellini）中，回忆了他与费德里科·费里尼的最后一次对话。这部由意大利Atomic和RAI Cinema出品的《最后的费里尼》……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "马丁·斯科塞斯在将于周六在罗马电影节首映的全新纪录片《最后的费里尼》（The Last Fellini）中，回忆了他与费德里科·费里尼的最后一次对话。该片聚焦这位意大利电影大师生前的最后十年。", "links": [{"text": "Martin Scorsese", "url": "https://variety.com/t/martin-scorsese/"}, {"text": "Federico Fellini", "url": "https://variety.com/t/federico-fellini/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《最后的费里尼》由意大利的Atomic和RAI Cinema联合制作，其国际发行权已被PiperPlay拿下。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "众所周知，斯科塞斯是费里尼的超级粉丝，曾将《8½》列为他有史以来最喜欢的电影之一。他的电影基金会也参与了费里尼杰作《甜蜜的生活》（La Dolce Vita）的修复工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "相关报道", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/tom-skerritt.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "曾出演《栅栏之爱》与《异形》的明星汤姆·斯凯里特逝世，享年93岁", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "曾出演《栅栏之爱》与《异形》的明星汤姆·斯凯里特逝世，享年93岁", "links": [{"text": "Tom Skerritt, 'Picket Fences' and 'Alien' Star, Dies at 93", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/news/tom-skerritt-dead-picket-fences-alien-1236921694/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管关于费里尼的故事已经讲过很多，但他生前的最后华章依然鲜为人知。《最后的费里尼》由詹路易吉·阿托尔（Gianluigi Attorre）执导，其中还穿插了对罗伯托·贝尼尼、作曲家尼古拉·皮瓦尼、记者温琴佐·莫利卡、漫画家米洛·马纳拉以及费里尼形影不离的秘书菲亚梅塔·普罗菲利（Fiammetta Profili）的采访，回顾了这位标志性导演在1980年代和90年代寻找项目资助变得更加艰难时所经历的挣扎。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《The Last Fellini》中，他详细讲述了他与费里尼如何差点合作拍摄一部他深情地称之为“疯狂”的纪录片系列，内容涵盖电影制作的各个方面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们有一个[片段]讲制片人；我们有一个讲演员；我们有一个讲摄像师，”剪辑师等等，斯科塞斯回忆起费里尼对他说的话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "带有幽默转折的是，费里尼还对斯科塞斯说，对于制片人而言，最重要的角色其实是外景经理。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "斯科塞斯回忆自己当时问：“我说，‘是吗，为什么呢？’”他说，‘因为当你去勘景时’——这本来是要写进剧本里的——‘无论你是去罗马、帕尔马还是其他什么地方勘景，外景经理都得知道哪里有靠近好餐馆的地方，这样你们才能停下来吃午餐。’……所以这才是最重要的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "斯科塞斯在片中讲述这段轶事时开怀大笑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "按计划，这部费里尼纪录片系列的第一部一小时短片将以演员为主题。当时与环球影业有合作协议的斯科塞斯已经筹集到了100万美元资金来资助它。但随后费里尼生病，并于1993年10月逝世。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当纪录片的叙事来到1993年——他生命的最后一年时，影片展现了费里尼在洛杉矶接受终身成就荣誉奥斯卡奖的场景。颁奖典礼的第二天，他与斯科塞斯进行了最后一次电话交谈，他将在下方片段中回忆这一幕。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“所以我接起电话，这一次他的声音非常虚弱，他只是说：‘谢谢你，马丁。谢谢你，谢谢。你知道的，我们很快会再见的。嗯，但愿如此。’”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随后，斯科塞斯开始猜测费里尼当时在谢什么，因为他们此前并没有直接谈及他已经找到了资金这件事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我不太确定，但他的声音非常虚弱，”斯科塞斯重申道。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Martin Scorsese recalls his last conversation with Federico Fellini in “The Last Fellini,” a new documentary about the final decade of the Italian auteur’s life premiering at Rome Film Festival on Saturday.

“The Last Fellini,” which is produced by Italy’s Atomic and RAI Cinema, has been picked up for international sales by PiperPlay.

Scorsese is well known to be huge Fellini fan and has cited “8½” as one of his all-time favorite films. His film foundation was also involved in restoring Fellini’s masterpiece, “La Dolce Vita.”

Related Stories

Tom Skerritt, 'Picket Fences' and 'Alien' Star, Dies at 93

Though much has been told about Fellini, the final chapter in his life remains largely unexplored. “The Last Fellini,” which is directed by Gianluigi Attorre — and also features interviews with Roberto Benigni, composer Nicola Piovani, journalist Vincenzo Mollica, comic book artist Milo Manara and Fellini’s inseparable secretary, Fiammetta Profili — looks at the iconic director’s struggles during the 1980s and ’90s when it became harder for him to find support for his projects.

In “The Last Fellini,” he details how he and Fellini almost teamed up on what he affectionately calls a “crazy” documentary series about different aspects of film production.

“We have one [segment] on the producer; we have one on the actor; we have one on the cameraman,” the editor and so on, Scorsese recalls Fellini telling him.

In a humorous twist, Fellini also told Scorsese that, for a producer, the most important role was that of the location manager.

“I said, ‘Yeah, and why is that?'” Scorsese remembers asking. “He said, ‘Because when you go location scouting’ — this was going to be in the script — ‘Whether you are scouting through Rome or Parma or wherever, the location manager has to know of a location that’s near the good restaurant, so you could stop and have lunch.’ … So that’s the main thing.”

Scorsese laughs heartily retelling this anecdote in the doc.

The plan was for the first one-hour segment of this Fellini documentary series to be on the actor. Scorsese, who had a deal with Universal at the time, had secured $1 million to finance it. But then Fellini became ill and died in October 1993.

As the doc’s narrative reaches 1993, his final year, it shows Fellini receiving an honorary Oscar for lifetime achievement in Los Angeles. The day after the ceremony, he had his last phone conversation with Scorsese, which he recalls in the below clip.

“So I pick up the phone, and this time his voice was very weak, and he just said, ‘Thank you, Martin. Thank you, thank you. You know, I’ll see you soon. Yeah, I hope so.'”

Scorsese then goes on to speculate on what Fellini was thanking him for, since they hadn’t spoken directly about the fact that he had found the financing.

“I’m not quite sure, but his voice was very weak,” Scorsese reiterates.
